name: Galway
title: Galway Ship Gauging: UTM for Tankers, Coasters & Tenders
description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging at Galway Docks and Galway Bay: product tankers, coasters, cruise tenders and research vessels, hull, tanks and piping.
h1: Ship Thickness Measurement at Galway Docks and in Galway Bay
intro: Galway is a small tidal dock on the west coast of Ireland, at the head of the bay, receiving petroleum products, bulk cargo and coastal traffic, with cruise ships anchoring off and landing passengers by tender. The port is modest, but its vessels are real working ships whose steel needs checking before survey dates and sales. A team travelling from India to Ireland gauges ships alongside the docks, at the bay anchorage or during a short lay-up.

highlights.h: A tidal dock that sets the clock
highlights.p: Galway is a tide-governed harbour, and ships enter and leave at the right state of tide. That fixes the length of any berth stay, so we plan a scope that fits the window and not one that hopes for extra time.

Short-sea ships bringing fuel, fertiliser and general cargo make up the working fleet. Their frequent calls make them practical candidates for staged gauging, a few tanks or the piping at a time, across successive visits.

highlights.h: Tendered cruise ships and research craft
highlights.p: Cruise ships lie in Galway Bay while their passengers go ashore by tender, and research and survey ships also use the bay. Their gauging is done at the anchorage or during planned lay-by periods, in cooperation with the master.

port.h: Galway Docks and the bay: a compact tidal port with a wide tidal range
p: Galway sits at the north-east corner of Galway Bay, an Atlantic inlet sheltered to the south by the Aran Islands. Galway Harbour Company runs the commercial docks at the mouth of the Corrib, reached by a dredged channel across shallow ground at the head of the bay. Shallow water and a wide spring range make tide and draught the controlling factors: large ships do not use the port, and the ones that do are timed to the water. Pilotage is compulsory for the commercial berths, and masters unfamiliar with the approach are glad of it.

Commercial traffic is made up of petroleum products, fertiliser, timber, aggregates and general cargo carried by coasters and small tankers. The trade is steady rather than heavy, and several of the ships that call are on regular rotations between Irish and UK ports. Cruise ships visit through the summer, but they anchor in the bay and send their passengers ashore by tender, since the dock itself does not suit their size. Galway also hosts research ships, patrol vessels and, from time to time, project cargo, and the Aran Islands ferry services run from nearby Rossaveal, not from the city docks.

Because the port is small and tidal, gauging here is a matter of fitting the work into the time a ship actually has. A coaster alongside to discharge a cargo of fuel or fertiliser may stay only a tide or two. A ship laid by between charters, or waiting for orders, can be on the quay for days. Anchorage work in the bay depends on sea state, and the exposed parts of the bay see swell from the southwest. Winter weather on this coast is the main reason a visit is scheduled with a reserve day.

facilities.h: Where gauging can be done at Galway
p: There is no drydock at Galway, and ships that need a docking go to a yard in another Irish port or across the sea. The port is therefore a place for in-service gauging: hull and deck structure from alongside, tank structure after cleaning, and machinery-space piping at any time the engine room is accessible. The commercial quays take ships for a tide or longer, and the port will normally allocate a berth near the cargo it is serving, which affects how much of the ship a team can reach.

For ships that wait in the bay, the anchorage becomes the working place. Launches are arranged through the agent, and the team boards in daylight when the sea allows. Cleaned tanks, void spaces and deck areas can then be gauged without taking up a berth. Lay-by berths on the quays suit longer jobs that need several days of uninterrupted access, such as a pre-purchase gauging programme, and an agent can say which berth the port is likely to offer in the period concerned.
list: Galway Docks commercial quays — hull, deck and tank gauging on coasters and small tankers during discharge, planned around the tide.
Fuel and bitumen discharge berths — piping and deck gauging on product tankers under the terminal's permit rules.
Lay-by berths at the docks — longer pre-purchase or off-hire condition gauging that needs several days on board.
Galway Bay anchorage — launch-borne gauging of cleaned tanks and deck structure on waiting ships, and tender-supported cruise ships.
Research and patrol vessel berths — hull, tank and piping checks on specialist ships between sailings.

context.h: Irish rules and the small-port context in Galway
p: Galway is subject to the same port state control regime as any Irish port, administered by the Marine Survey Office under the Paris MoU. Small ships and coasters often feel inspection more sharply than large ones because their structure is lighter, and a visible record of recent readings helps a manager show that wastage is under control. Charterers and buyers of older coasters ask for measured thickness before they commit, so Galway jobs are often triggered by a commercial event as much as by a survey date.

EU requirements apply in full: ships calling here must hold an Inventory of Hazardous Materials, and the EU ETS and FuelEU Maritime frameworks apply to larger ships on voyages to and from Irish ports. For smaller ships, the practical effect is the same as everywhere else in the Union, which is that an older hull is judged against the cost of a replacement. Class societies set the survey schedule, and a ship that has its steel measured early in the cycle has more choice about when to carry out repairs.

jobs.p: Jobs at Galway are small to medium and are shaped by the tide. A scope is agreed with the master or superintendent in advance, with priority areas first and extra spaces added if time permits. The team brings only the equipment the scope needs, and the report goes out in the format the class surveyor or the buyer's surveyor expects. Where a ship is bound for a docking elsewhere, the data is formatted so the yard can use it directly in its estimate.
list: Pre-docking gauging on a coaster, covering deck plating, hatch coamings and the accessible ballast tanks.
Piping and deck structure gauging on a small product tanker during a short discharge call.
Pre-purchase condition gauging on an older general cargo ship laid by at a lay-by berth.
Anchorage gauging of cleaned tanks on a cruise or research vessel during a planned call.
Intermediate survey preparation on a coastal ship on a regular Irish Sea rotation.

logistics: Shannon Airport is the closest international airport and Dublin is the other usual gateway, with a road transfer to Galway. Technicians travel from India on Irish visas, applied for when the ship's visit dates are known, and we allow margin for the tide and the weather. Port access, quay permits and launches for anchorage work are arranged through the ship's agent, who also confirms the berth the port has allocated for the call.
vessels: Coasters and short-sea general cargo ships

faqs.q: Is it worth gauging a small coaster at Galway?
faqs.a: Often it is, because the survey or sale decision for a small ship depends on a few areas of steel that readings can clear or confirm. A short, focused programme of hull, deck and a handful of tanks can be done in a tide or two. The report tells the owner what is sound and where renewals are likely.

faqs.q: How does the tide affect the work at Galway Docks?
faqs.a: The tide decides when a ship can enter and leave, so it limits how long it stays alongside. We build the scope around the expected berth time and prioritise the areas the survey or the buyer cares about most. If a ship lies over, the plan is extended to further spaces, and the report records what was and was not reached.

faqs.q: Can a cruise ship be gauged while it is at anchor in Galway Bay?
faqs.a: In part. A cruise ship that anchors for the day can have engine-room piping, scrubber lines and prepared tanks gauged while passengers are ashore, provided the master agrees and the sea state allows a launch. It is a partial picture that works best as one stage in a programme spread over several calls.

faqs.q: Where does a ship go for a docking if it trades through Galway?
faqs.a: There is no drydock in the port, so ships dock at a yard in another Irish or UK port, or further afield. We can gauge at Galway beforehand and give the yard measured thickness ahead of arrival, which reduces uncertainty in the steel estimate and lets repair quotations be agreed before the ship is in dock.
